units.text: برای تولید داده دانلود به‌صورت درخواستی در `st.download_button`، مطابق مستندات نسخه 1.52.0 که در 3 دسامبر 2025 منتشر شده، می‌توانید یک تابع قابل فراخوانی (callable) به پارامتر `data` بدهید. این تابع در زمان کلیک روی دکمه اجرا می‌شود و داده‌های تازه تولید شده را برمی‌گرداند. منبع هشدار می‌دهد که این قابلیت ممکن است در همه نسخه‌ها یا محیط‌ها سازگار نباشد و تضمین نمی‌کند که همیشه تأخیرها را به‌طور کامل رفع کند.

طبق مستند منبع، از نسخه 1.52.0 به بعد امکان پاس دادن یک callable به پارامتر `data` در `st.download_button` وجود دارد که دادهٔ دانلود را هنگام درخواست و به شکل on-demand تولید می‌کند. این روش بهترین الگوی مستند شده برای کاهش مسدودسازی اسکریپت هنگام تولید دادهٔ بزرگ است. محدودیت این روش در مستند آن نسخه ذکر شده و بیان شده که تضمینی برای رفع همه تأخیرها نیست.

initial_candidates.title: Enhance menu button with download payload capability
initial_candidates.text:
### Why?

Today, `st.menu_button` only communicates **which option was selected** on the rerun where the user picks something; **sending bytes to the browser still requires `st.download_button`** (or other workarounds). In practice that causes:
- **Awkward UX**: pick a format from the menu, then click again to download—or rely on `st.session_state` because the menu’s return value resets on later reruns.
- **Repeated boilerplate**: every app reimplements mapping from “format label” → `data` / `file_name` / `mime`.
- **Cost vs. laziness**: precomputing every variant (e.g. large PDFs or zips) wastes CPU and memory; deferring generation until after a choice fights Streamlit’s rerun model unless authors invent their own patterns.
A combined primitive would match common product UI, reduce custom session-state hacks, and make multi-format export easier to build and maintain.

initial_candidates.title: caching
initial_candidates.text:
#### Usage
Let's look at an example of using `st.cache_data`. Suppose your app loads the [Uber ride-sharing dataset](https://github.com/plotly/datasets/blob/master/uber-rides-data1.csv) – a CSV file of 50 MB – from the internet into a DataFrame: ```python def load_data(url): df = pd.read_csv(url) # 👈 Download the data return df df = load_data("https://github.com/plotly/datasets/raw/master/uber-rides-data1.csv") st.dataframe(df) st.button("Rerun") ``` Running the `load_data` function takes 2 to 30 seconds, depending on your internet connection. (Tip: if you are on a slow connection, use [this 5 MB dataset instead](https://github.com/plotly/datasets/blob/master/26k-consumer-complaints.csv)). Without caching, the download is rerun each time the app is loaded or with user interaction. Try it yourself by clicking the button we added! Not a great experience… 😕 Now let's add the `@st.cache_data` decorator on `load_data`: ```python @st.cache_data # 👈 Add the caching decorator def load_data(url): df = pd.read_csv(url) return df df = load_data("https://github.com/plotly/datasets/raw/master/uber-rides-data1.csv") st.dataframe(df) st.button("Rerun") ``` Run the app again. You'll notice that the slow download only happens on the first run. Every subsequent rerun should be almost instant! 💨

initial_candidates.text:
### How?

Ship either a **new widget** (for example `st.download_menu_button`) or an **extension** of `st.menu_button` / `st.download_button` so one control can:
1. Show a dropdown of export labels.
2. On selection, trigger a download using the **payload mapped to that label**.
**Options API (sketch for discussion)**
Accept a structured mapping instead of plain string labels only, for example:
- A **list of tuples or small dicts**, e.g. `(label, file_name, mime, data)`; or  
- A **dict** keyed by label with values like `{ "data": ..., "file_name": ..., "mime": ... }`.
**Lazy payloads**
Allow `data` (or the equivalent field) to be a **callable** that Streamlit invokes **only when that option is chosen**, so expensive exports are not built on every rerun. Document when the callable runs, error handling, and any constraints (e.g. serialization, size limits).

initial_candidates.text:
### Debug info

- Streamlit version: 1.52.2
- Python version: 3.13
- Operating System: Win
- Browser: Chrome

Somehow I missed this issue https://github.com/streamlit/streamlit/issues/13337
Closing as duplicate

Confirming this from a production incident — and it's a bit worse than "missing ScriptRunContext produces a warning": inside that thread, `st.session_state` reads return stale values and `@st.cache_data`-wrapped calls silently return whatever was already cached, **with no error and no warning**. Both just look like they worked.

Our incident: a `data=callable` on `st.download_button` called into functions that (transitively) read `@st.cache_data`-cached helpers. Because those calls run outside `ScriptRunContext`, they picked up cached results from a *different* request context — users occasionally downloaded a file that didn't match what they'd just generated on screen, with nothing in the logs to explain why. We only found the mechanism by tracing the full call graph of the callable, not just inspecting it — a lambda that looks pure can still be unsafe if anything it calls touches cached/session state indirectly.

We ended up moving off lazy `data=` entirely (eager bytes, pre-warmed at save time) because we couldn't make the callable's dependency tree provably free of session/cache reads. For anyone hitting this: if your callable calls anything that isn't a pure function of its arguments, the missing context isn't just a perf/warning issue, it's a correctness one.
